summary: This memo describes the Internet Gopher protocol, a distributed document search and retrieval system built around menus, along with an overview of how to implement clients and servers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet Gopher protocol lets a client browse and retrieve documents from different servers through simple menu entries. This memo describes the request and response format and the item types that clients can recognize.

questions: how does a gopher menu work
subtitle: A menu-based protocol for finding and retrieving documents from distributed servers.

tldr.problem: Users needed a simple way to browse documents and services held on many independent servers.
tldr.mechanism: A client connects over TCP, sends a selector line and receives a directory or document. Menu entries provide an item type, display name, selector, host and port.
tldr.outcome: Gopher presents a network of linked information sources through a simple request and response format. RFC 1436 is Informational and does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 1436 is an Informational memo published in March 1993. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: A Distributed Document System
sections.content:
Gopher is designed to deliver documents and services held on many servers. A client presents these items in a hierarchy resembling a file system, so a user can browse directories and select items without needing to know which machine holds them.

The format is intentionally simple. The RFC says this makes it easier to implement and debug clients and servers, including on small desktop systems. Servers can extend the available services through item types.
sections.plainLanguage: Gopher lets a user browse a list of documents even when those documents live on different computers. The client shows the names, while the server details tell the client where to request each item.

sections.title: A Request and Response
sections.content:
A Gopher client connects to a server over TCP and sends a selector, which is one line of text and may be empty. An empty selector asks the server to list its available items. A server replies with a text block that usually ends with a period on a line by itself, then closes the connection.

The server retains no state between transactions. To retrieve an item from a menu, the client connects to the host and port in that entry and sends its selector. The selector is opaque to the client and must not be changed.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a line that identifies what it wants. The server returns a document or a list of items, then closes the connection.

sections.title: Directory Entries and Item Types
sections.content:
A directory entry starts with a type character, followed by a display name, a TAB, a selector, a TAB, a host name, a TAB and a port. The client displays the name and uses the selector, host and port to retrieve the item. Extra tab-separated fields may be ignored by a basic client.

Type 0 identifies a file, 1 a directory and 7 a search service. Other defined types include phone-book, binary-file, image and Telnet entries. For binary types 5 and 9, the client reads until the TCP connection closes rather than waiting for a period terminator.
sections.plainLanguage: Each directory line gives the client a type, a name to show, and the information needed to fetch the item. The type tells the client whether the entry is a file, a directory, a search or another service.

sections.title: Links, Search and Gateways
sections.content:
Gopher links can point to servers anywhere on the Internet, so the information structure is a graph and need not be a tree. An institution may use a well-known top-level server, but the RFC does not require every secondary server to register through it. Registered server aliases can help clients continue to find a service if it moves.

A search server accepts a selector and search words, then returns a directory-like list of matching documents. Gateway servers can translate between Gopher and other retrieval services, allowing an unmodified Gopher client to reach them. The RFC places most service-specific intelligence in the server rather than in the basic protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A Gopher menu can point to another server, and that server can point elsewhere. A search server returns matching items as a menu, while a gateway connects Gopher to another service.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's Security Considerations section states that security issues are not discussed in this memo. It defines a document retrieval protocol and does not specify security protections for the retrieved information.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo does not discuss security or define protections for information retrieved through Gopher.
